content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has established comprehensive guidelines for the declaration of interests among its experts, as outlined in its 2014 publication. These guidelines are critical for ensuring transparency and integrity in the development of health policies and recommendations. In 2007, WHO introduced principles and processes for integrating its reproductive health guidelines and tools into national programs. This document emphasized the importance of adaptation and implementation strategies tailored to specific country contexts. The WHO guidelines for the treatment of genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) were developed with input from regional STI focal points and experts across various WHO regions. These regions include the Americas (AMR), Europe (EUR), the Western Pacific (WPR), Africa (AFR), South-East Asia (SEAR), and the Eastern Mediterranean (EMR). Key contributors from each region provided expertise and guidance to ensure the guidelines addressed global and regional needs. The guideline development process involved a multidisciplinary team, including experts in reproductive health, HIV/AIDS, maternal and child health, and epidemiology. Notable contributors included Massimo Ghidinelli (AMR), Lali Khote (EUR), Ying-Ru Lo (WPR), Frank Lule (AFR), Razia Pendse (SEAR), and Hamida Khattabi (EMR), among others. These individuals represented diverse fields and brought a wealth of knowledge to the guideline development process. The WHO headquarters team, including members from the Department of Reproductive Health and Research, played a central role in coordinating the development of these guidelines. Key contributors included Moazzam Ali, Avni Amin, Rachel Baggaley, Venkatraman Chandra-Mouli, Jane Ferguson, Mario Festin, Mary Lyn Gaffield, Antonio Gerbase, Sami Gottlieb, Frances McConville, Lori Newman, Annette Mwanza Nkowane, Anita Sands, Igor Toskin, Marco Vitoria, Ian Askew, Nathalie Broutet, James Kiarie, Lee Sharkey, and Teodora Elvira Wi. The guideline development process was led by Teodora Elvira Wi, with methodological support from Nancy Santesso and her team at McMaster University. This team conducted systematic reviews and applied clinical epidemiology principles to ensure the guidelines were evidence-based and robust. The systematic review team, led by Nancy Santesso, included members such as Housne Begum, Janna-Lina Kerth, Gian Paolo Morgano, Kristie Poole, Nicole Schwab, Matthew Ventresca, Yuan Zhang, and Andrew Zikic. Their work was instrumental in synthesizing evidence to inform the recommendations. The guidelines prioritized four categories of sexually transmitted infection (STI) conditions based on their global importance and the need for updated recommendations. These categories included conditions previously addressed in the 2003 WHO STI guidelines, new conditions identified for inclusion, rare conditions with limited new evidence, and conditions covered in other national guidelines but not selected for inclusion in the updated WHO guidelines. The guideline development group (GDG) held a meeting in December 2013 to discuss and finalize the list of population, intervention, comparator, and outcome (PICO) questions. These questions guided the systematic review process and ensured that the guidelines addressed the most critical aspects of STI management. The GDG also conducted surveys among its members to rank the importance of populations, interventions, and outcomes for each STI condition. This prioritization process ensured that the guidelines focused on the most relevant and impactful areas of STI prevention and treatment. The guidelines were informed by a review of existing international guidelines, including those from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH), the Public Health Agency of Canada, the International Union against Sexually Transmitted Infections (IUSTI), and national guidelines from Australia, South Africa, and India. The WHO guidelines for the treatment of genital herpes simplex virus represent a collaborative effort involving experts from around the world. These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to improve the prevention, diagnosis, and management of genital herpes and other STIs globally.
